title: Cap. II: Faustus — initiative, progress, election from foresight merits
pass_a_gloss: Concerning the prior striving and labor Faustus writes in book 1, chapter 12: Just as it is of his own crime that the prodigal son fled far from the eyes of a pious parent, so it is of his own devotion that, deliberating and rising through the good implanted in him, he runs back to the paternal embraces. And chapter 17: The Lord invites the willing, draws the desiring, raises the striving. And the last chapter: He waits for the will of him who is to be purged. Concerning progress and perseverance through the powers of free choice, not through some special gift flowing from the decree of predestination, he philosophizes thus, book 2, section 5: He has placed the salvation of a human not in the Maker's predestination, but in the operation of the one serving the Giver of grace. And chapter 12: A human's state can turn in diverse ways not according to God's constitution, but according to the liberty of choice. Finally he openly teaches our election from the foresight of such a good will and operation of ours, not from some antecedent decree of God, book 2, section 2: God's foresight takes its beginning from the matter of human acts. And a little after: It is one thing to foresee, another to predestine. Foresight knows beforehand what is to be done; afterward predestination describes what is to be repaid. That foresights merits; this preordains rewards. Foresight pertains to power, predestination to justice. Unless foresight has explored, predestination decrees nothing. By these words he does not fetch merits from the grace of predestination, but predestination from foresight merits. Key lemmas: Faustus; conatus praevius; praescientia / praedestinatio; merita praevisa.
pass_b_english: On that prior effort and labor Faustus writes (1.12): just as the prodigal's flight from a pious father's eyes is his own crime, so his return to the father's embrace — deliberating and rising by the good planted in him — is his own devotion. Chapter 17: the Lord invites the willing, draws the desiring, raises the striving. The last chapter: he waits for the will of the one to be cleansed. On progress and perseverance by free choice's powers — not by any special gift flowing from the predestination decree — he reasons (2.5): human salvation is set not in the Maker's predestination, but in the working of the one who serves the Giver of grace. Chapter 12: a person's state can turn this way or that not by God's constitution, but by liberty of choice. At last he openly teaches election from foresight of such good will and working of ours, not from any prior decree of God (2.2): God's foresight begins from the matter of human acts. A little later: to foresee is one thing, to predestine another. Foresight knows beforehand what is to be done; then predestination marks out what is to be repaid. That foresights merits; this preordains rewards. Foresight belongs to power, predestination to justice. Unless foresight has searched, predestination decides nothing. In these words he does not draw merits from the grace of predestination — he draws predestination from foresight merits.
source_text: De praevio conatu & labore scribit Faustus lib. 1. cap. 12. Sicut sui criminis est, quod filius prodigus longe pii parentis fugit oculos, ita suae est devotionis, quod per insitum sibi bonum deliberans & assurgens, ad paternos recurrit amplexus. Et cap. 17. Dominus invitat volentem, attrahit desiderantem, erigit adnitentem. Et cap. ult. Voluntatem ejus qui est purgandus, exspectat. De progressu & perseverantia per vires liberi arbitrii, non per donum aliquod speciale manans a decreto praedestinationis, sic philosophatur, Lib. 2. sect. 5. Salutem hominis non in praedestinatione Factoris, sed in operatione famulantis largitor gratiae collocavit. Et Cap. 12. Status hominis in diversa, non pro constitutione Dei, sed pro arbitrii libertate potest versari. Denique electionem nostram ex praescientia hujusmodi bonae voluntatis & operationis nostrae, non ex Dei decreto aliquo antecedente, aperte docet lib. 2. sect. 2. Praescientia Dei de materia humanorum actuum sumit exordium. Et paulo post, Aliud est praescire, aliud praedestinare. Praescientia gerenda praenoscit, postmodum praedestinatio retribuenda describit. Illa praevidet merita, haec praeordinat praemia. Praescientia ad potentiam, praedestinatio ad justitiam pertinet. Nisi praescientia exploraverit, praedestinatio nihil decernit. Hisce verbis non a gratia praedestinationis arcessit merita, sed a praevisis meritis praedestinationem.
